chunks.text: The true ashoka (Saraca asoca) is a small, erect evergreen tree in the subfamily Detarioideae of the legume family Fabaceae, native to the Indian subcontinent from Pakistan across India, Bangladesh and Myanmar, and from Nepal and Bhutan south to Sri Lanka. It naturally grows in seasonally dry tropical forest, historically concentrated on the Deccan Plateau and in the Western Ghats. The tree has deep green leaves in dense clusters, and blooms from roughly February to April in heavy, fragrant bunches of flowers that open bright orange-yellow before turning red as they wilt. Wild populations have become increasingly rare, and the species is classified as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, though scattered wild specimens are still found in the Himalayan foothills, the northern Indian plains and near Mumbai on the west coast; the tree is also widely cultivated as an ornamental in temple and palace gardens. The bark is a traditional medicinal plant in Ayurveda.

chunks.source: Wikipedia — Saraca asoca (mythology and religious significance)
chunks.text: The ashoka is worshipped in the Hindu month of Chaitra and is associated with Kamadeva, the god of love, whose quiver of flower-arrows includes an ashoka blossom said to induce a kind of seductive hypnosis. In the Ramayana, the Ashoka Vatika (grove) in Lanka is the garden of ashoka trees where Hanuman finds Sita held captive. Buddhist tradition holds that Queen Maya gave birth to the Buddha beneath an ashoka tree. The yakshi figure standing beneath an ashoka tree is a recurring motif in ancient Hindu and Buddhist sculpture, which some scholars trace back to older tree-and-fertility deity imagery. The ashoka flower is the state flower of Odisha. It is frequently confused with the unrelated 'false ashoka,' Polyalthia longifolia, which is commonly planted as an avenue tree and differs from the true ashoka in its leaf shape, apple-green (rather than red) flowers and fruit.
